hypotheses.claim: The JPQL query scans millions of rows due to a missing index on paid_date, causing heavy DB work per request.
hypotheses.mechanism: PaymentRepository.findByPaidDate translates to a SELECT filtering on paid_date without an index, forcing MySQL to perform a full range scan over ~19 M rows each call, consuming ~19 ms of DB CPU/I/O per request.
evidence: server‑side SQL time 1915.2 ms for 100 requests → ≈19.15 ms per request (≈75.74 % of 28.1 ms p50)
rows examined / rows sent = 19 911 200 / 10 000 → ~1 991× more rows scanned than returned
SQL audit flags [MISSING_INDEX] and reports 51 301 rows examined to return 50 rows
hypotheses.prediction: Creating an index on payment(paid_date) will drop the per‑request SQL time from ~19 ms to <1 ms and the overall latency will fall accordingly.

hypotheses.claim: The service loops over each projection row, creates a DTO and adds it to a list, incurring per‑row allocation and copy work.
hypotheses.mechanism: PaymentsByDateService.byDate receives the JPQL projection list, iterates over each element, copies fields into a response DTO and adds it to a new List before returning; each iteration performs object allocation and method calls.
evidence: p50 latency rises from 5.4 ms (1 row) to 8.8 ms (100 rows) → ≈0.034 ms per extra row
SQL time stays ~0.2‑0.3 ms, so the extra ~3.4 ms is non‑SQL
hypotheses.prediction: Returning the repository list directly without the extra DTO mapping loop will reduce the per‑row latency increase by roughly 3‑4 ms for 100 rows.

hypotheses.claim: Jackson serialises each DTO to JSON (and the server may gzip it), adding a per‑row CPU cost.
hypotheses.mechanism: Spring MVC uses the Jackson HttpMessageConverter to write the List of DTOs to the HTTP response; each object is turned into JSON text and then compressed, costing time proportional to the number of rows.
evidence: Response body size scales linearly: 72 B per row (1 row → 72 B, 100 rows → 7261 B)
Latency per row (~0.034 ms) matches typical Jackson cost for small POJOs
hypotheses.prediction: Disabling Jackson (e.g., returning a pre‑built JSON string or switching to application/octet‑stream) will eliminate the per‑row ~0.03 ms cost and flatten latency growth with row count.

probes_run.result: Latency 5.4 ms, SQL 0.2 ms, rows 1, body 72 B – baseline constant overhead; shows that most of the 5 ms is not SQL, hinting at framework/logic/serialization cost.
Latency 8.8 ms, SQL 0.3 ms, rows 100, body 7261 B – latency rises ~3.4 ms with 99 extra rows, confirming a linear per‑row cost separate from SQL.
Latency 8.1 ms, SQL 2.0 ms, rows 100, body 7443 B – higher SQL time but similar total latency, reinforcing that most extra cost is still non‑SQL per‑row work.
